turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. Obs are done. Blood pressure was one thirty-eight over eighty-four, pulse was ninety-two... no, eighty-eight, I rechecked it. Sats ninety-four percent on room air, respiratory rate eighteen, temperature thirty-six point eight.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. What's the problem?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Um, the cough. Mornings, mainly. And I get short of puff walking up to the shops.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long for the cough?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Last winter, or the one before. I can't put a date on it.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Every morning?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. Soon as I get up, about twenty minutes, then it eases off.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Wheeze with it?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No wheeze.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bringing up phlegm?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): A bit of grey stuff in the morning. Not much. Not green now.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blood?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fever?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Not now. I was crook though, a few weeks back. Or last month. I don't know, doctor, the dates are a blur.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): What was that illness?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Green phlegm, and the cough got worse. The clinic gave me antibiotics and it settled. Mostly.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which antibiotic, and for how long?
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): Amoxicillin, five hundred milligrams, three times a day. For a week... no, five days. I finished the pack.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Green phlegm gone?
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah, gone. Just that grey bit in the mornings again.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Breathless at rest?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Flat ground I'm alright. Hills, I have to stop halfway.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ankles swelling?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Still smoking?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. About ten a day... maybe twenty. Depends on the day. I lose count, I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): How many years have you—
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Since I was sixteen, or thereabouts. Forty years? Could be longer. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Sorry, my head went to the parking meter. It's only an hour out there. Doesn't matter.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Inhalers?

[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Blue one, salbutamol, when I'm puffed. And the brown preventer, beclomethasone. Meant to be twice a day. I forget, few times a week if that. I'm hopeless with it, I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Strength of the salbutamol?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): A hundred micrograms? Maybe. Two puffs. I don't know, doctor, the label's rubbed off.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the brown one?
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Two hundred micrograms, two puffs, twice a day. That's what's printed. I just don't do it.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Other tablets?
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Amlodipine for the blood pressure. Ten milligrams... no, five. They cut it down. Once a day.

[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): My sister's mad on biotin, keeps leaving her bottle at my place for her hair. I don't take it. And the bloke next door is on metformin for his sugar, always comparing notes. Not my problem.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Medicine allergies?
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Mum said penicillin gave me a rash as a kid. I'm not sure it was a real allergy. I've steered clear of it anyway.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Night-time wheeze? You said none.
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): Well, actually, yeah. There is a whistle in the chest, mornings, and if I walk up the hill. I didn't reckon that was wheeze. Sorry.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Shirt up, I'll have a listen.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hyperinflated chest. Scattered wheeze both sides, louder on the right. No crackles. Heart sounds normal. No ankle oedema.

[SEG0048] person_1 (NURSE): Spirometry from earlier. FEV1 was one point nine litres... sorry, one point six four litres, fifty-eight percent predicted. FVC three point one litres, ratio fifty-three percent. After the puffer, FEV1 one point seven two, only a small rise.

[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): That pattern is airflow obstruction. Working impression is COPD, with the smoking and the morning cough. Not confirmed till the X-ray's back. Could also be leftover from that infection.
[SEG0050] person_3 (PATIENT): COPD. Right. Um, is that bad? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's manageable if you treat it. Chest X-ray this week.

[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll switch the brown inhaler to budesonide with formoterol. I was going to use the four hundred over twelve, no, the two hundred over six, two puffs twice a day. Keep salbutamol for breakthrough. Stop the beclomethasone so you don't double the steroid.
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): Every day? I already forget the brown one.
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): Every day, that's the instruction. And the cigarettes have to go. I'm referring you to Quitline.
[SEG0055] person_3 (PATIENT): Quitline. Yeah. I've tried before and, um, I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): Patches only if you set a quit date. Not writing them today.
[SEG0057] person_1 (NURSE): I can book the X-ray downstairs for Thursday morning, and I'll send the Quitline referral through this afternoon.
[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in six weeks with the result. If the breathlessness gets worse or you cough up blood, come in sooner.
[SEG0059] person_3 (PATIENT): Six weeks. What if it's still just that infection? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0060] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's what the X-ray is for. If it's not settling we might send a sputum sample, not today.
[SEG0061] person_3 (PATIENT): And I keep the blue puffer? My sister'll be annoyed I'm not taking her biotin.
[SEG0062] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep the salbutamol, two puffs when you need it. Biotin does nothing for your lungs. We're done.

spec.situation: Long-term smoker with morning cough and breathlessness; minimises smoking ('about ten a day... maybe twenty'), inhalers used irregularly, a recent chest infection; spirometry numbers read aloud; quitting support offered.
features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
